frictionVectors.title: European gas leverage
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons and export infrastructure, but European buyers are pressing for pricing flexibility and additional supply amid shifting energy markets.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel border instability
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Mali, Libya, and Niger increases military and border-security costs while complicating Algeria's effort to preserve strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese lending, Western infrastructure partnerships, and Gulf investment continue to shape access to ports, railways, and minerals, limiting Luanda's room for fully independent policy.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito mineral corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: U.S. and European support for the corridor strengthens Angola's bargaining position but exposes critical infrastructure to geopolitical competition over Congolese and Zambian copper and cobalt.

highlights: Cotonou remains a regional trade gateway

frictionVectors.title: Niger corridor confrontation
frictionVectors.details: Strained relations with Niger have disrupted established trade and energy routes, including the operating environment around Niger's oil exports through Benin.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist attacks and cross-border insecurity in the northern departments threaten roads, agricultural production, and state control near Burkina Faso and Niger.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers partnership renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has improved its negotiating position over diamond marketing and beneficiation, but remains exposed to the commercial health and strategic decisions of De Beers.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Synthetic stones, weaker global demand, and dependence on diamond revenues constrain fiscal autonomy and increase pressure to develop new minerals and downstream industries.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector nationalization drive
frictionVectors.details: The junta is expanding state participation, local processing, and oversight of gold exports, but informal mining and smuggling continue to divert value from public coffers.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Closer reliance on Russian-linked security support reduces Western influence but creates new dependency risks, while jihadist violence still restricts access to mining zones and transport routes.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and Smuggling
frictionVectors.details: Gold and rare-earth production remain vulnerable to informal export networks and opaque licensing, limiting state capture of value. Regional insecurity and weak border controls amplify outside commercial influence.

frictionVectors.title: Transport and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi relies heavily on neighboring countries and external financiers for ports, roads, fuel, and electricity access. This dependence constrains policy autonomy despite efforts to diversify export corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Port and Tourism Assets
frictionVectors.details: External investors and development lenders remain central to port, airport, tourism, and renewable-energy projects. These inflows improve capacity but leave strategic infrastructure exposed to creditor and concessionaire leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Burden
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's Atlantic location makes it a partner in counter-narcotics and maritime surveillance operations led by outside powers. Security cooperation strengthens sovereignty but can narrow independent control over maritime priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon and Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and opaque concession structures retain substantial influence over oil, gas, timber, and emerging mining assets. Governance weaknesses limit domestic value capture and fuel elite-centered resource politics.

frictionVectors.title: Chad-Cameroon Pipeline Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The pipeline and associated export infrastructure remain vital to national revenues while tying Cameroon to external operators, lenders, and regional production risks. Any disruption would quickly pressure fiscal stability and energy security.

frictionVectors.title: Security Concessions and Mining Access
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security actors retain strong influence around regime protection and mineral access, especially gold and diamonds. The arrangement reduces some immediate security dependence while weakening transparency and state-wide control over extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-Group Control of Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Rebel and criminal networks continue to contest mining zones, roads, and border crossings. This fragments customs authority and enables illicit exports through neighboring states.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Revenue and External Operators
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues remain the backbone of state finance, but production, infrastructure, and marketing depend heavily on foreign operators and external buyers. Limited transparency and high security spending weaken broad-based resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Borderland Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Conflict spillover from Sudan and instability across the Sahel strain Chad's border control and redirect public resources toward military priorities. External security partnerships provide leverage but risk reinforcing dependence on foreign patrons.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and French control
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest French sovereignty over Mayotte, while the island's migration controls and maritime boundaries constrain Comorian territorial claims and resource access.

frictionVectors.title: Port and connectivity dependence
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and development financing rely heavily on external partners, leaving strategic transport and energy projects vulnerable to donor priorities.

highlights: Eastern security crisis undermines state control

frictionVectors.title: Mining leverage and contract sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain a dominant position in copper and cobalt, while Kinshasa seeks greater transparency, local processing, and renegotiation of major resource agreements.

frictionVectors.title: M23, Rwanda, and mineral corridors
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east links armed-group financing, cross-border trade, and mineral access, limiting Kinshasa's effective control over territory and transport routes.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues remain central to fiscal stability, exposing Brazzaville to price volatility and limiting diversification of sovereign resource control.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese project and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and resource relationships provide essential capital but deepen external influence over strategic assets and repayment priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire remains a leading cocoa producer but captures limited downstream value, leaving farmer incomes and export policy exposed to foreign processors and global buyers.

frictionVectors.title: French and Gulf infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: French firms remain influential in strategic infrastructure while Gulf and other investors expand in ports, logistics, and energy, creating leverage competition around national assets.

frictionVectors.title: Base concentration and sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generate revenue and leverage but make Djibouti's security and foreign policy closely tied to external powers.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Strategic ports and corridors are vital to the economy, yet heavy reliance on external financing and regional trade flows creates vulnerability to debt, competition, and disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and asset concessions
frictionVectors.details: Debt, currency pressure, and reliance on Gulf and international financing are increasing outside influence over strategic assets and infrastructure. Privatization and investment deals can improve liquidity while narrowing policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian control over Nile flows and seeks a binding operating framework for the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. The dispute remains a persistent security risk despite diplomatic engagement.

highlights: Malabo seeks gas and mining diversification

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil and gas output leaves the state dependent on foreign operators, technical capital, and volatile export revenues. Production-sharing arrangements limit domestic control over the remaining resource base.

frictionVectors.title: Port and offshore infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Strategic ports and offshore energy infrastructure attract interest from external powers, particularly China and Western commercial actors. The government seeks diversification without surrendering control of maritime assets.

highlights: Mining revenues under tight state control

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb expose it to competition among regional and extra-regional powers. Foreign military activity nearby increases strategic value while raising sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide important revenue but rely heavily on foreign capital, technology, and offtake arrangements. Limited transparency makes the distribution of benefits and environmental costs difficult to assess.

frictionVectors.title: Regional infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies on South Africa for major transport corridors, energy interconnections, financial services, and market access. This creates practical leverage for Pretoria without requiring direct political intervention.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and trade exposure
frictionVectors.details: The sugar industry depends on preferential access to external markets and imported industrial inputs. Changes in European, regional, or US trade arrangements could materially reduce sovereign economic room.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam expands Ethiopia's electricity and bargaining power but remains a core source of tension with Egypt and Sudan. Disagreement over filling, drought management, and data sharing remains unresolved.

frictionVectors.title: Port access and regional corridors
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's landlocked status drives efforts to secure dependable access through Djibouti and other Red Sea routes. Corridor negotiations are entangled with Somali sovereignty concerns, regional competition, and external infrastructure financing.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon is seeking greater state participation and local processing in manganese and other minerals, but Chinese, French, and other foreign firms remain central to capital, technology, and export logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Transition-Era Institutional Risk
frictionVectors.details: The post-Bongo political order has strengthened executive control while leaving uncertainty over civilian oversight, contract stability, and the long-term distribution of resource revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Cross-Border Economic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for transport connectivity, energy, trade access, and regional security, limiting its room for independent infrastructure and resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: Industrial Fishing Encroachment
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked industrial fleets and weak monitoring continue to threaten coastal fisheries, a strategic food and livelihood resource, despite efforts to improve licensing and enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Environmental Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining and disputes involving foreign-backed operators are degrading water systems and farmland, forcing Accra to balance investor confidence against stronger domestic control over gold resources.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF programs, creditor negotiations, and dependence on foreign investment continue to shape fiscal, energy, and infrastructure choices, limiting short-term policy independence.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Foreign Consortiums
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project is drawing major Chinese, Singaporean, Emirati, and other external interests, while rail and port infrastructure could lock Guinea into long-term export dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Revenue Imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Guinea remains a major bauxite exporter but captures limited value through local processing, with environmental damage and opaque contracting fueling sovereignty concerns during military rule.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Export Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on raw cashew exports and external buyers, leaving farmers and state revenues exposed to price manipulation, logistics bottlenecks, and limited domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Narcotics Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and recurring political crises leave ports and maritime routes vulnerable to transnational trafficking networks and foreign influence, undermining effective control of national infrastructure.

highlights: Strategic balancing between China, Gulf investors, and Western lenders
Ports, power, and debt remain sovereignty pressure points

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is diversifying financing partners, but Chinese-linked infrastructure obligations and IMF-backed fiscal reforms constrain policy autonomy. Control of major logistics and energy assets remains politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Northern corridor insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability around the Somalia border threaten transport corridors and raise reliance on foreign security assistance.

highlights: Water exports anchor dependence on South Africa
Textiles and mining face external market vulnerability

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water revenues are strategically important, but dependence on South African infrastructure, payments, and demand limits its bargaining power over a core national resource.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-owned production base
frictionVectors.details: The garment sector and emerging mining operations remain heavily dependent on foreign capital and preferential market access, leaving employment and revenues exposed to external decisions.

highlights: Mining and port concessions dominate the sovereignty debate
Debt relief has improved fiscal room but not resource leverage

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mineral concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining companies control major production and logistics interests, while the state continues to face pressure to improve revenue capture, local processing, and environmental enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and key infrastructure depend on external operators and financiers, limiting Liberia's ability to convert strategic access into broad domestic industrial capacity.

highlights: Oil wealth remains divided among rival power centers
External sponsors shape security and export stability

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented oil governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing authorities, armed groups, and disputes over the central bank and National Oil Corporation continue to threaten unified control of production revenues and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and energy influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked networks, regional states, and European actors retain leverage through security partnerships, migration policy, and energy interests.

highlights: Critical minerals attract intense foreign competition
Energy deficits weaken domestic value capture

frictionVectors.title: Mining concession tensions
frictionVectors.details: Large nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and graphite projects bring export revenue but generate recurring disputes over taxation, environmental damage, land rights, and the limited domestic processing base.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and power dependence
frictionVectors.details: Madagascar relies on donors, foreign investors, and imported fuel while its unreliable electricity system constrains sovereign industrial development and bargaining power.

highlights: Fuel and fertilizer supply remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Mining-contract asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking investment in rare earths, uranium and graphite, but limited fiscal capacity and weak bargaining power increase the risk of concessions delivering modest domestic value.

frictionVectors.title: Import chokepoint vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported fuel, fertilizer and foreign exchange leaves the country vulnerable to external price shocks, transport disruptions and lender conditionality.

highlights: Security partnerships are being rapidly realigned

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector sovereignty push
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are tightening control over industrial mining and seeking a larger state share, generating friction with foreign operators while raising expectations for domestic revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security realignment
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal from Western security frameworks and deeper reliance on non-Western partners has increased operational autonomy but also exposed Mali to sanctions, diplomatic isolation and logistics risks.

highlights: Gas exports open a new fiscal chapter
Atlantic logistics are becoming strategic assets

frictionVectors.title: Offshore gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project can improve state revenues and regional leverage, but its cross-border structure and foreign-operated infrastructure limit immediate sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral corridor concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and port revenues remain concentrated around externally financed rail and maritime systems, leaving Mauritania exposed to commodity cycles and foreign capital decisions.

highlights: Indian Ocean sovereignty is being consolidated

frictionVectors.title: Chagos settlement implementation
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is strengthening its sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago, but future arrangements around Diego Garcia and wider-power security interests will constrain policy space.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: As a trade, finance and logistics hub, Mauritius remains sensitive to shipping disruptions and external control of digital, port and energy infrastructure.

highlights: Phosphates and corridors anchor regional influence

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses phosphate, fisheries and renewable-energy development in Western Sahara to reinforce territorial claims, while recognition disputes and legal challenges complicate external investment.

frictionVectors.title: External capital dependence
frictionVectors.details: Automotive, hydrogen, ports and renewable projects expand sovereign capacity but remain reliant on European, Gulf and multinational finance, technology and market access.

highlights: LNG Restart Hangs on Cabo Delgado Security

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado LNG Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to threaten the security perimeter around major gas investments and delay full project resumption. Foreign energy operators retain substantial leverage over timelines, financing, and security arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Mega-Project Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Graphite, rubies, and natural-gas projects generate foreign exchange but provide limited near-term domestic control over value chains. Maputo faces pressure to increase local content while preserving investor confidence.

highlights: Oil and Green Hydrogen Recast the Economy
Walvis Bay Becomes a Strategic Gateway

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries have attracted major international operators, creating opportunities for state revenue but also raising questions over licensing transparency, environmental safeguards, and domestic participation.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Led Green Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Green-hydrogen and port projects depend heavily on external capital, technology, and export markets. Namibia is seeking stronger local ownership and industrial spillovers without slowing project development.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is pursuing greater control over uranium and other extractive assets while reducing French influence. Production, investment, and technical capacity remain vulnerable to diplomatic rupture and insecurity.

frictionVectors.title: Benin Oil Pipeline Dispute
frictionVectors.details: The export pipeline to the Beninese coast is strategically vital but exposed to political tensions, border restrictions, and security disruptions. Niger's landlocked position sharply limits its bargaining autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Delta Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, vandalism, and militant activity continue to reduce production and public revenue. International oil companies remain important operators, while government enforcement and community agreements produce uneven results.

frictionVectors.title: Refining and Fiscal Dependence
frictionVectors.details: New domestic refining capacity could strengthen energy sovereignty, but crude supply, fuel pricing, foreign exchange shortages, and debt obligations constrain the transition. The state remains exposed to global oil-price volatility.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral Flows
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's mineral-trading and logistics networks face persistent international scrutiny over alleged links to conflict minerals and armed-group financing in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Diplomatic pressure could affect exports, investment, and regional access.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Traceability
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda is expanding formal processing and traceability for tin, tantalum, and tungsten, but its landlocked economy remains dependent on neighboring corridors and external buyers. Strong state control improves administrative capacity while limiting independent oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Exploration Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon prospects remain commercially uncertain, while exploration depends heavily on foreign capital and technical expertise. The government faces pressure to secure better terms without discouraging investment.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Infrastructure Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: High dependence on imported fuel and limited grid capacity constrain economic sovereignty. External partners, including Portugal, China, and multilateral lenders, remain important for infrastructure financing.

frictionVectors.title: Contract Renegotiation Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater national participation and transparency in oil, gas, and mining arrangements. Renegotiation efforts risk litigation, investor caution, and tension with established international operators.

frictionVectors.title: GTA and Regional Coordination
frictionVectors.details: The shared Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas project with Mauritania requires sustained bilateral coordination over revenue, infrastructure, and maritime jurisdiction. Production growth could strengthen fiscal autonomy but also deepen dependence on foreign operators and markets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Maritime Influence
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from security and infrastructure ties with India, China, and Western partners, but must avoid becoming overdependent on any one external actor. Port access, maritime surveillance, and defense cooperation remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and Climate Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing access and limited enforcement capacity challenge control over marine resources. Climate impacts and debt exposure also constrain the country's ability to capture full value from tourism and the blue economy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dominance
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects remain central to export earnings but are largely controlled by foreign firms and exposed to commodity-price volatility. The government is pressing for more local value addition and stronger fiscal returns.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining logistics depend on externally financed roads, ports, and power infrastructure. Contract terms and infrastructure concessions can improve connectivity while limiting domestic control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Maritime Security
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, Western partners, and regional actors retain major roles in training, basing, port development, and maritime security. This support is essential but fragments national control over strategic infrastructure and coastal waters.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Licensing and Federal Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Emerging offshore and onshore petroleum activity is vulnerable to disputes between the federal government and member states over licensing, revenue sharing, and ownership. Weak institutions and persistent insurgency increase the risk that external firms capture disproportionate value.

highlights: Electricity and logistics remain binding constraints

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is balancing Chinese processing investment, Western critical-minerals initiatives, and domestic beneficiation goals. Regulatory uncertainty and infrastructure bottlenecks limit its leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and rail degradation
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and freight-rail failures undermine mineral exports and industrial sovereignty. Private-sector participation is expanding, but fiscal and governance constraints slow recovery.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-route dependency
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on export infrastructure crossing Sudan, leaving production vulnerable to war, pipeline disruption, and external bargaining. Oil revenues remain central while diversification is minimal.

frictionVectors.title: External security and financial leverage
frictionVectors.details: Regional states, foreign oil firms, and humanitarian actors retain major influence over security and economic access. Weak institutions and elite competition limit sovereign control over resources.

highlights: Red Sea access becomes strategic prize

frictionVectors.title: Competing external patrons
frictionVectors.details: The SAF-RSF war is sustained by foreign financing, arms networks, and political backing, turning gold, agriculture, and logistics corridors into instruments of influence. National institutions have little effective control over extraction zones.

frictionVectors.title: Port and gold-route contest
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan, gold flows, and Red Sea access carries outsized strategic value for regional and global actors. Infrastructure damage and blockade risks threaten remaining state revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and LNG bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pressing for greater local content, fiscal returns, and processing from foreign mining and gas investors. Delays and disputes can improve state leverage but also deter infrastructure finance.

frictionVectors.title: Port and transport competition
frictionVectors.details: Dar es Salaam and the Central Corridor are attracting competition from Gulf, Chinese, and Western-backed logistics interests. Tanzania is using this rivalry to diversify partners while protecting strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: Port dependency and foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: Lomé port and associated logistics networks rely heavily on external finance, operators, and regional trade flows. This expands revenue potential but creates exposure to foreign commercial and political leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security corridor
frictionVectors.details: Militant spillover from the Sahel is increasing pressure on northern Togo and its transport links. Security partnerships must balance Western, regional, and other external actors without compromising strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European financial and diplomatic support remains linked to Tunisia's cooperation on migration control, creating sovereignty concerns over border policy.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported fuel and constrained investment in domestic energy infrastructure leaves Tunis vulnerable to external price and financing pressures.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Ownership
frictionVectors.details: The crude export pipeline to Tanzania remains central to Uganda's resource strategy but exposes the country to foreign capital, environmental scrutiny, and sanctions-related pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and contracting support major transport and energy projects while increasing long-term repayment and procurement dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf-linked investors for copper and cobalt assets gives Zambia leverage, but foreign control of capital and processing remains substantial.

frictionVectors.title: Debt Restructuring Constraints
frictionVectors.details: External debt negotiations and IMF-linked reforms restrict fiscal room for state-led infrastructure, industrial policy, and stronger domestic participation in mining.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mineral Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign investors remain prominent in lithium, platinum, and gold, while domestic processing capacity and transparent revenue capture lag behind resource extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Currency Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and persistent currency instability increase reliance on external suppliers, lenders, and informal markets, weakening the state's practical control over strategic resources.
